profile.name: logobi
profile.tagline: The Abidjan street dance of martial strikes, big arms, and rapid footwork.
profile.insight: Known as 'la danse des gros bras', logobi turned martial arts and street-gang fight mimes into an acrobatic dance form that migrated from Abidjan ghettos to Parisian commuter stations.
profile.profile: Logobi is an urban dance and musical style born in the 1980s in the popular quarters and university campuses of Abidjan, Côte d'Ivoire. Dubbed 'la danse des gros bras', it translates street combat, martial arts stances, and secret gang codes into swift arm gestures and jerky footwork. Closely intertwined with traditional zouglou and later influencing coupé-décalé, it expresses social realities of hardship and aspirations for justice. In the late 2000s, West African diaspora crews in France hybridized logobi with tecktonik and electro beats, staging battles across suburban rail hubs.
profile.profile_long:
Emerging in 1986 across the popular quarters of Abidjan—most notably the working-class ghetto of Abobo—and circulating through university campuses, logobi arose as a distinct street dance rooted in the culture of urban loubards (gang members). The term 'logobi' derives from Nouchi, the Ivorian street slang, translating to 'making oneself crafty' or earning money through cunning and trickery. While drawing structural roots from traditional zouglou, logobi adopted a raw, aggressive posture, codified by martial artist and gang leader John Pololo (Sahiri Gnédré Lazare), who fused genuine combat gestures with contemporary percussive music.

The physical execution of logobi earned it the popular epithet 'la danse des gros bras' ('the dance of big arms'). It is distinguished by rapid, expressive upper-body movements, jerky footwork, and literal mimes of street altercations. Dancers simulate martial arts strikes, knife or weapon handling, secret hand signals, and bravura posturing interspersed with sexual gestures. The performance reflects both the daily violence of poverty and a collective yearning for peace, survival, and prosperity.

During the late 2000s and early 2010s, logobi experienced an energetic cross-continental evolution when youth of the West African diaspora brought it into the suburbs of Paris. Gathering in public squares, metro stations, and transit hubs like Gare du Nord or Châtelet, crews staged dance battles that merged logobi's percussive foundation with elements of electro dance, Belgian hard-tech, and tecktonik. French groups such as Logobi GT streamlined the raw gang aesthetics into energetic pop choreography suitable for a younger generation, charting club hits across Europe.

Musically, logobi operates over rapid tempos, relying on percussive Coupé-décalé instrumentals, traditional zouglou drums, or compressed electronic club tracks. In Abidjan, it fills neighborhood maquis and outdoor block parties, while retaining an improvisational core where dancers trade solos. Revitalized on contemporary social media platforms like TikTok by artists like Samo Samo, logobi remains an enduring kinetic vocabulary of Ivorian street resilience.

sections.origins_and_history: Logobi appeared in Côte d'Ivoire in the 1980s (specifically traced to 1986), spreading across the working-class ghettos of Abidjan, particularly Abobo, as well as university campuses. It grew out of the loubard (street gang) subculture. Urban lore and diaspora accounts credit John Pololo (Sahiri Gnédré Lazare, 1962–2000), a martial artist and leader of the gang 'Vagabons Sauvés' (VS), as its inventor and codifier who fused martial arts movements with street music.
sections.how_it_is_danced: The dance is characterized by rapid, highly expressive arm maneuvers—giving it the nickname 'la danse des gros bras'—alongside jerky, staccato footwork. Dancers improvise movements inspired by street combat, martial arts punches, secret gang signals, weapon handling, and sexual gestures. Performances range from spontaneous maquis and block party circles in Côte d'Ivoire to competitive crew battles held in public transit stations.
sections.music_and_instruments: Logobi is danced to fast-tempo music with high rhythmic speed. Musical accompaniments include zouglou rhythms, fast-paced coupé-décalé instrumentals, and heavily compressed electronic beats. In its European adaptation, it incorporated French tecktonik and Belgian hard-tech electronic sounds.
sections.costume_and_setting: Historically practiced in the street environments, maquis (open-air restaurants/bars), and university campuses of Abidjan, it requires no formal ceremonial dress. In its French diaspora phase, it took place in train stations, subways, and shopping malls among street crews dressed in contemporary urban wear.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: Derived from the Nouchi concept of getting by through cunning and street smarts, the dance communicates the social realities of poverty, misery, and street struggle while voicing hope for prosperity, peace, and justice. It serves as both street bravado and social expression.
sections.notable_figures: Key figures include John Pololo (Sahiri Gnédré Lazare), who codified the dance; musical groups and artists such as Logobi GT, Les Youlés, Yang Systeme, Les Mantanien, Samo Samo, Les Garagistes, Espoir 2000, Magic System, Petit Yodé and l'Enfant Siro, Molière, Petit Denis, Gor la Montagne, and Moussier Tombola; and visual artist Christelle Oyiri (CrystallMess), who documented the Parisian movement.
sections.regional_variants: The original Ivorian variant is grounded in loubard street culture, zouglou, and raw martial arts pantomime. The French diaspora variant, which emerged in Parisian banlieues, infused the style with tecktonik, electric club textures, and hard-tech, softening the explicit gang imagery for broader youth and club audiences.
sections.lineage: Logobi evolved out of traditional Ivorian zouglou dance and loubard martial culture during the 1980s. It predated and influenced the emergence of coupé-décalé in the early 2000s, later hybridizing with European electronic dance genres in France before experiencing social media revivals.

profile.sacred_note: Logobi is a secular urban street dance and musical movement; it contains no sacred or restricted religious elements.

basic_steps: Stance: Adopt a balanced, grounded street posture with knees slightly bent and core braced for rapid weight shifts.
Gros Bras Pump: Drive clenched fists or open palms out in rapid forward and crossing thrusts, mimicking boxing strikes and martial arts blocks.
Jerky Footwork (Jeux de jambes): Step in quick, staccato, syncopated pulses, snapping the feet under the hips to match high-tempo electronic or coupé-décalé beats.
Combat Mime: Integrate stylized street-gang gestures, including defensive parries, simulated weapon draws, and defiant hand signals.
Freestyle Break: Loosen into expressive isolations, incorporating pelvic accents or dynamic foot sweeps within a freestyle cypher.
teaching.rhythm: Fast, high-energy syncopated 4/4 meter driven by high-tempo coupé-décalé or electro-house percussion.
teaching.formation: Solo improvisation within an open circle (cypher), street-corner gathering, or facing crew battle.
teaching.level_notes: Beginners should focus on upper-body arm coordination and speed before layering in the rapid, jerky footwork.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Rapid syncopated West African snare and bass kicks layered over compressed four-on-the-floor or coupé-décalé rhythmic grooves.
music_profile.vocal_style: Energetic Nouchi street chanting, hype calls, melodic hooks, and rapid-fire spoken phrases.
music_profile.musical_form: Vamp-based verse-chorus arrangements structured around driving instrumental drops and battle breaks.
music_profile.sound_description: A high-velocity sonic assault driven by digital kick drums, snappy snare syncopations, and repetitive synthesizer riffs. In its traditional form it relies on heavy Ivorian percussive grooves, while modern diaspora iterations layer buzzy electro synths and hard-tech compression.

movement_profile.posture: Grounded, athletic, and ready to spring, with flexed knees and forward-tilted torso evoking martial arts readiness.
movement_profile.footwork: Saccadic, jerky steps and rapid weight transfers under a stable center of gravity.
movement_profile.arms_and_hands: Violent, rapid arm thrusts, boxing parries, flexed bicep displays ('gros bras'), and coded gang signals.
movement_profile.hips_and_torso: Tightly coiled core with sharp torso twists and periodic provocative or sexual hip overtures.
movement_profile.formation_and_space: Open street cypher, station concourses, or opposing battle lines with explosive forward excursions.
movement_profile.partnering: Primarily solo within a battle or group context; non-contact adversarial face-offs.

signature_moves.name: Les Gros Bras
signature_moves.description: Rapid, forceful flexes and thrusts of the arms simulating martial arts strikes and physical intimidation.

signature_moves.name: Jeux de Jambes Saccadés
signature_moves.description: Quick, staccato foot shifts executed in double-time beneath a mobile upper body.

signature_moves.name: Mime de Combat
signature_moves.description: Theatrical street-fight pantomime, including dodging, striking, and brandishing simulated weapons.

movement_profile.levels_and_jumps: Primarily mid-level athletic stance with sudden drops, defensive crouches, and sharp vertical hops.
movement_profile.what_to_avoid: Avoid turning fight mimes into genuine physical contact; do not perform without maintaining the underlying percussive bounce.

episode_brief.title_hook: The Dance of Big Arms: From Abidjan Ghettos to Parisian Stations
episode_brief.logline: Born from the martial arts codes of Ivorian street gangs, logobi transformed urban survival into a high-octane dance phenomenon spanning West Africa and Paris.
beats: Open in Abobo, Abidjan, where loubard youths turned martial arts training into a physical language of defiance in the 1980s.
Profile John Pololo, the charismatic street figure who fused combat techniques with zouglou rhythms to codify logobi.
Demonstrate the anatomical core of 'la danse des gros bras': rapid fist strikes, defensive parries, and staccato footwork.
Shift to the late 2000s in Paris: diaspora teens bringing logobi into train concourses like Gare du Nord, merging it with tecktonik.
Examine the viral resurgence on TikTok in 2025-2026 led by artists like Samo Samo.
Conclude with a high-energy cypher illustrating how an art born of urban poverty continues to demand recognition and joy.

lesson_ladder.goal: Master the balanced, low-center combat stance and baseline bounce.
drills: Find a wide, grounded squat with elbows tucked and fists guarded.
Pulse in half-time to a fast coupé-décalé beat, keeping heels mobile.
Shift weight side-to-side without elevating head height.

lesson_ladder.goal: Execute rapid martial arm strikes and blocks in syncopated tempo.
drills: Throw alternating straight punches snapping back instantly to guard.
Execute crossing forearm blocks while maintaining the foot bounce.
Chain four strikes into an overhead bicep flex on the final accent.

lesson_ladder.goal: Combine jerky footwork with pantomime fight gestures at full speed.
drills: Drill staccato shuffle footwork beneath alternating punch sequences.
Incorporate a sudden dodge, drop level, and recover into a street mime gesture.
Freestyle an 8-count routine alternating aggressive strikes with open theatrical posturing.

visual_motifs: Dust kicking up under sneakers on unpaved Abidjan streets.
Gleaming tiled floors and harsh neon lights of Parisian commuter train stations.
Muscular arm flexes captured in sharp slow-motion against fast percussion.
Archival footage of Abidjan university rallies and 1980s loubard gatherings.
episode_brief.instructor_persona: An energetic urban street dancer from Abidjan who balances sharp martial discipline with infectious, charismatic humor.
episode_brief.music_cue: Start with a dry, acoustic zouglou percussion loop that abruptly kicks into a full-throttle 140 BPM electronic beat.

connections.name: zouglou
connections.note: Logobi developed directly out of zouglou on Abidjan university campuses, adding martial and street elements.

connections.name: coupé-décalé
connections.note: Logobi preceded and influenced coupé-décalé, which later provided the fast electronic instrumentals often used to dance logobi.

connections.name: tecktonik
connections.note: Logobi absorbed tecktonik and electro elements during its diaspora evolution in the Parisian banlieues.

gaps: Specific formal footwork syllabus or step names beyond 'jeux de jambes saccadés' and martial combat mimes are not detailed in the sources.
Exact BPM ranges are not given numerically in sources; described qualitatively as 'tempos rapides' and 'rythme élevé'.

claims.text: Logobi first appeared in Côte d'Ivoire in 1986 and spread through Abidjan university campuses.
claims.quote: It first appeared in Côte d'Ivoire in 1986 and was popularized initially in university campuses in Abidjan.

claims.text: Logobi literally means in Nouchi slang to earn money through cunning, crafty means or trickery.
claims.quote: The literal meaning of "logobi" in Nouchi (an Ivorian slang) is to earn money through cunning, crafty and often trickery means to earn a fortune.

claims.text: The dance incorporates fight moves, weapon handling, gang signals, and sexual overtures.
claims.quote: Many of the dance moves accompanying the music are depictions of bandits, hooligans and street gangs, including fight moves, use of weapons, secret gang signals and sexual overtures.

claims.text: The style is nicknamed 'la danse des gros bras'.
claims.quote: It has also been dubbed "la danse des gros bras" (literally, the dance of big arms).

claims.text: The dance is characterized by fast, expressive arm movements, jerky footwork, and street-fight mimes.
claims.quote: Il se caractérise par des mouvements de bras rapides et expressifs (d’où son surnom de « danse des gros bras »), des jeux de jambes saccadés et des mimes inspirés des combats de rue.

claims.text: John Pololo is recognized as the inventor or codifier of logobi, combining combat gestures and music.
claims.quote: Plusieurs sources ivoiriennes et de la diaspora le présentent comme le codificateur ou l’inventeur du Logobi, qu’il aurait développé en mélangeant gestuelle de combat et musique.

claims.text: In France, crews formed and used public spaces such as train stations, metros, and malls for battles.
claims.quote: Des crews se forment et investissent les espaces publics (métros, gares, centres commerciaux) pour des battles et des démonstrations.

claims.text: French logobi merged coupé-décalé percussion with tecktonik and Belgian hard-tech sounds.
claims.quote: il fusionne les rythmes percussifs du coupé-décalé avec les sonorités frénétiques de la tecktonik et du hard-tech belge.

claims.text: Logobi GT helped popularize this version with songs like Un Bail Ke Yes and Elle danse sexy.
claims.quote: Le groupe Logobi GT (formé à Champigny-sur-Marne) joue un rôle important dans la popularisation de cette version auprès d’un public plus large, avec des titres comme Un Bail Ke Yes ou Elle danse sexy.

claims.text: Logobi was revived on social platforms by artists like Samo Samo in 2025-2026 with titles like Logobi and Faut Gbâchi.
claims.quote: En Côte d’Ivoire, des artistes comme Samo Samo relancent le style en 2025-2026 avec des titres viraux (Logobi, Faut Gbâchi)
